title: Customer consent flow and tiny-audit playbook (PRD draft)
content:
Purpose:
Short: propose a compact, customer-first approval + audit design ("tiny-audit") for private deployments that minimizes customer egress, keeps forensic fidelity for incidents, and preserves operator consent semantics for VPC-managed networking.

Background / motivation:
- Customers running Redwood Private frequently request the ability to control networking (e.g., customer-managed NAT, firewall, peering) while still getting meaningful audit evidence from Redwood for regulatory and support purposes.
- Full verbose audit logs (every packet, every request body) are both expensive to store/transfer and create privacy/regulatory surface area for customers who prefer minimal copies leaving their VPC.
- We need a pattern that: 1) gives customers control, 2) provides Redwood SRE/Support with replayable evidence when authorized, 3) satisfies compliance teams (retention, tamper-evidence), and 4) keeps operational cost low.

Goals (what success looks like):
1) Define an approval flow UX and API for customer-managed network changes that requires explicit operator consent scope for Redwood to access audit evidence.
2) Design a compact audit artifact format ("tiny-audit") that is:
   - cryptographically verifiable (digest chain),
   - size-bounded (target: <= 1KB/event averaged after compression for common events),
   - supports replay-level pointers (evidence pointers to on-prem attachments or short-lived presigned blobs),
   - configurable retention/escrow per-customer and per-jurisdiction.
3) Provide a developer-friendly contract (API + example SDK) and an SRE runbook for emergency access and forensics.

Non-goals:
- Full packet-capture or deep packet inspection in-host.
- Replacing customer SIEM; tiny-audit is meant to be Redwood's compact evidence capsule, not a full observability mirror.

Key concepts (lexicon):
- Operator consent: explicit approval from a named customer operator binding a time window and evidence scope (read-only, hashed-only, presigned-blob-access).
- Tiny-audit bundle: compressed event(s) with metadata, cryptographic chain anchor, optional pointer(s) to customer-hosted evidence.
- Approval gate: policy predicates (role, time-window, risk-score, change-type) evaluated client-side and echoed to Redwood's control plane for authorization records.

Design overview:
1) Approval flow (UX + API):
   - Customer operator initiates a VPC/network change in their console (customer-side UI) or via API (customer-controlled).
   - Change request sent to Redwood control plane with a proposed evidence scope ID (e.g., minimal-hash, audit-full, evidence-pointer-only).
   - Customer operator signs consent with their key (KMS/HSM-backed) and sets: allowed-read-window (e.g., 7 days), permitted-actors (list of Redwood roles), and emergency-escalation-contact.
   - Redwood validates signature and stores the consent record as an immutable ledger entry (consent-id).
   - If policy requires human review, consent is held in a pending state until approver signs.

2) Tiny-audit artifact format (compact event capsule):
   - Fields (flat): event_id, timestamp, event_type, actor_id, brief_summary (<= 240 chars), digest_anchor (sha256 base64), evidence_pointers (0..n short URLs), retention_policy_id, consent_id, signature_by_agent (optional).
   - All text fields are UTF-8; the whole capsule is compressed (zlib) and then base64-encoded for transport.
   - Digest chain: each capsule includes digest_anchor which is sha256 of: (previous_digest || capsule_payload). This creates an append-only chain for per-tenant evidence.
   - Evidence pointers are typically short-lifetime presigned URLs hosted inside the customer's VPC (e.g., s3 presigned with customer-owned key) or references to encrypted blobs in Redwood escrow (if customer opted-in).

3) Customer privacy modes (configurable):
   - Minimal (default): only hashed/summary artifacts are exported to Redwood. Evidence pointers omitted. Redwood can request access, but will require a new signed consent.
   - Escrowed: customer configures an encrypted escrow bucket; tiny-audit capsules include pointer to encrypted blob (AES-256) in Redwood-managed storage with customer KMS-wrapped keys. Access requires consent-id and an audit-authorization token.
   - Full-share: customer explicitly opts to share full artifacts for a specified time window for SRE/troubleshooting.

4) Approval gate predicates (examples):
   - change_type in {egress-rule, peering, nat-config} AND actor_role == network-admin -> auto-approve if within maintenance window.
   - change_type == peer-add AND risk_score >= 0.7 -> require human approver + second-signature.
   - cross-jurisdiction changes -> trigger legal-review flagging and extended retention.

5) Forensic access model and emergency path:
   - Normal: Redwood Support may request decryption/presigned access with consent-id; request is routed to customer's operator for approval. All attempts are recorded in the ledger.
   - Emergency (severe incident): preconfigured emergency-escalation rules (signed at onboarding) can allow time-limited break-glass with multiple approvers and out-of-band verification. Post-event, the event is audited and requires business-owner signoff.

Operational & compliance considerations:
- Retention tiers: ephemeral (7d), short (30d), standard (365d), legal-hold (indefinite). Customer selects default and can override per-change during consent.
- Tamper evidence: digest chain and immutable ledger entries (consent records) anchored periodically (e.g., weekly) to a public transparency log (we will prototype using a Merkle root anchor).
- Cost model: smaller events reduce egress + storage. Escrowed encrypted blobs stored in Redwood escrow incur storage costs; propose explicit billing line for escrow retention.
- Jurisdiction controls: evidence pointers must include geo-claims; we enforce that presigned blobs for EU-only data stay in EU regions.

Developer contract / API sketch (examples):
- POST /v1/private/vpc/changes
  payload: {change, evidence_scope_id, metadata}
  headers: {Customer-Signature}
- GET /v1/private/audit/consent/{consent_id}
- POST /v1/private/audit/request-access {consent_id, reason}

SDK helper: sign_consent(consent_payload, kms_key_ref) -> Customer-Signature header value.

Runbook for SRE & Support:
- Steps to request evidence: create support ticket -> include consent_id -> request_access call -> wait for operator sign-off OR follow emergency-escalation path.
- Verification checklist: validate digest chain anchor, verify signature on consent record, verify evidence pointer expiry and integrity.

Migration & rollout plan:
- Phase 0 (internal): implement tiny-audit capsule producer in staging for 2 customers (experimental).
- Phase 1 (alpha): opt-in for existing Private customers, collect feedback on capsule size and content.
- Phase 2 (beta): default to Minimal with easy opt-in to Escrowed for new customers.
- Phase 3 (GA): provide formal SLAs for consent escrow and emergency access windows.

Open questions / tradeoffs:
- How much structured context to include in tiny-audit (e.g., end-user identifier vs hashed identifier)? Privacy vs utility tradeoff.
- Anchor cadence for Merkle anchoring: daily vs weekly (cost vs detectability).
- Presigned pointer standard: short URL length limit, rotation strategies for long-running investigations.
- Escrow KMS model: customer-managed keys (bring-your-own-key) vs Redwood-managed keys with customer wrap.
- Billing UX for escrowed storage: single line item vs per-event billing.

Next steps / immediate work items:
- ENG: prototype capsule schema + chain anchoring (GH-privnet/audit-indexer#22) - owner: Ethan. ETA: 2 sprints.
- PRODUCT: prototype consent UI and developer API contract draft - owner: Priya. ETA: end of sprint.
- SRE: draft emergency escalation playbook and runbook for access approval - owner: Marcus. ETA: 3 weeks.
- LEGAL/SEC: review retention tiers and cross-border pointer policy - owner: Olivia. ETA: 2 weeks.

Notes to self / rough ideas to capture:
- Consider optional differential snapshots: store only deltas for network ACL changes to keep size down.
- Think about integrating with customer SIEM via webhook for immediate copy-on-write when configured.
- We should draft a short customer-facing one-pager describing the tiny-audit tradeoffs and how to set the privacy mode.
- Track related tickets: ENG-4127, LEG-88, CS-243.

End.
